Author Names: Nouha Arfaoui
Title of the Paper: Enhancing Machine Learning Algorithms for Imbalanced Data—A Case Study: Spam Detection
Dataset Used: SpamAssassin Public Corpus (Kaggle): easy_ham 2,551; hard_ham 250; spam_2 1,397. easy_ham + hard_ham are combined as ham; spam_2 is spam.
Methodology Used: Text preprocessing with tokenization, stop-word removal and lemmatization; stratified 80/20 split; CountVectorizer and TF-IDF; six balancing methods (SMOTE, BorderlineSMOTE, RandomUnderSampler, TomekLinks, SMOTEENN, SMOTETomek); classifiers include MultinomialNB, LinearSVC, KNN, Decision Tree, Logistic Regression, Random Forest and Gradient Boosting; GridSearchCV and RepeatedStratifiedKFold used for robust evaluation.
Limitation of the Paper: No dedicated limitations section is provided. The experimental scope is limited to one SpamAssassin corpus and accuracy is the primary evaluation metric, so cross-corpus generalization is not demonstrated.

Author Names: Worawit Kitikusoun; Nawaporn Wisitpongphan
Title of the Paper: Adaptive Semi-Personalized Email Classification Model (ASPEC) with Incremental Learning
Dataset Used: Anonymized real corporate email-server logs from a large Thai financial-services enterprise: 625,069 emails across 3 months and 9,788 employees in 12 functional departments. 423,043 emails used for training/testing; 202,026 for incremental-learning evaluation.
Methodology Used: ASPEC uses privacy-preserving email metadata rather than body content. Classical ML models (Logistic Regression, Decision Tree, Random Forest) are combined with adaptive feature selection and group-level model selection based on occupational and behavioral context. Models are periodically updated using batch-incremental learning to adapt to changing communication patterns.
Limitation of the Paper: No direct comparison with transformer/deep-learning models; body content is excluded because only metadata is used; current grouping may need extension for very large enterprises; evaluation is from a single organization and limited time period, so cross-organization generalizability remains unvalidated.

Author Names: Zhiyong He; Chang Liu; Boyang Hu; Duo Jia
Title of the Paper: SpamLLM: Leveraging Large Language Models for Robust Spam Email Classification
Dataset Used: Four public spam benchmarks: SpamAssassin, LingSpam, SMSSpamCollection and CSDMC2010.
Methodology Used: Multimodal SpamLLM framework combines structured email metadata, body statistics, raw body text and attachment metadata. Numerical features are normalized, categorical features frequency-encoded, and text is represented with TF-IDF plus deep semantic features from a frozen LLaMA-3.1-8B backbone. Fused representations are processed by a lightweight classification head; training uses Adam with the LLM frozen, plus efficiency techniques such as FP16 and precomputed embeddings.
Limitation of the Paper: Evaluated on four relatively small/static benchmarks; adversarial spam, multilingual spam and cross-domain generalization were not empirically validated; freezing the backbone limits domain adaptation; the 8B-parameter model still has substantial memory and inference-latency requirements.

Author Names: Sahar Hamad Ahmed; Hadeel M. Saleh; Sameer Alani
Title of the Paper: Enhanced Email Spam Filtering Using Spectral Clustering and Deep Neural Networks
Dataset Used: Enron Email Dataset; SpamAssassin Dataset; UCI Mail Spam Dataset.
Methodology Used: Proposes SCDNN, combining spectral clustering with deep neural networks. Spectral clustering partitions the email corpus into neighborhood/centroid-based groups, then a DNN performs spam classification using distance/likelihood information. The approach is compared with backpropagation neural networks, SVM, Random Forest, Bayesian methods and other standard classifiers using accuracy, precision, recall and F1-score.
Limitation of the Paper: The authors state that further investigation is required for complex deployment scenarios such as cloud computing and real-time systems, and that the method still needs optimization for big-data settings.

Author Names: Dharmaraj R. Patil
Title of the Paper: Real-time Spam Email Filtering with Stacking and Majority Voting Ensembles
Dataset Used: Kaggle Email Spam Dataset.
Methodology Used: NLP preprocessing removes HTML tags, special characters, URLs and stopwords and applies lemmatization. Text is converted using TF-IDF and CountVectorizer. Base classifiers are Logistic Regression, Decision Tree, SVM and Stochastic Gradient Descent; their predictions are combined using stacking and majority-voting ensembles. Evaluation uses accuracy, precision, recall, F-measure, FPR and FNR.
Limitation of the Paper: Performance depends strongly on training-data quality and diversity; stacking/voting add computational overhead; large-scale deployment introduces scalability challenges; static training data can become outdated as spam evolves; surface-level features can miss nuanced, obfuscated or semantically complex spam.

Author Names: Abdulhanan Sharafat; Samet Aymaz; Cemal Köse
Title of the Paper: A Hybrid CNN-BiGRU-Attention Architecture for Enhanced Spam Email Classification
Dataset Used: TREC 2007 Public Spam Corpus (75,419); Enron-Spam (33,716); Spam-Assassin (5,796); Ling-Spam (2,893).
Methodology Used: Email headers are removed and body text is normalized; URLs, email addresses and numbers are replaced with placeholders; text is lowercased and tokenized with a 10,000-word vocabulary, padded to 250 tokens, and represented with pretrained GloVe embeddings. The hybrid architecture combines CNN for local lexical/n-gram features, BiGRU for bidirectional long-range dependencies and an attention mechanism for salient tokens. Evaluation includes stratified holdout, five-fold cross-validation and external cross-dataset validation.
Limitation of the Paper: Performance degrades under domain shift in cross-dataset testing; robust deployment would require more diverse multi-source corpora, domain adaptation or periodic retraining. Public labeled spam corpora are largely historical because of privacy constraints and may not reflect modern spam. Attention weights are not treated as post-hoc explanations.

Author Names: Mahmoud E. Ali; Anjali Diwan; Rajendrasinh Jadeja
Title of the Paper: Binary Spam Detection Using GRPO and LoRA on Qwen 2.5-3B-Instruct
Dataset Used: SpamClassify (5,572); SpamDetection (10,900); LingSpam (2,893); SpamAssassin (10,749).
Methodology Used: Fine-tunes Qwen 2.5-3B-Instruct for spam/ham classification using 4-bit quantization, LoRA and Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO). Datasets are standardized into instruction prompts with stratified train/test splits. Reward functions strongly reward correct classification and single-word outputs while penalizing wrong or verbose responses; GRPO uses grouped samples, reward scoring, relative advantage estimation and policy updates.
Limitation of the Paper: The study is limited to binary spam classification; multilingual, domain-specific, multiclass and multilabel settings remain untested. The reward design intentionally sacrifices explanatory responses in favor of one-word labels, and future work is needed across other model architectures and domains.

Author Names: Shruti Raju Mahitkar
Title of the Paper: Explainable AI-Based Spam Email Classification System
Year of Published: 2026 (PDF metadata; publication year not stated in article text)
Dataset Used: Publicly available spam datasets plus user-submitted emails; the paper does not identify exact dataset names.
Methodology Used: Email text is cleaned by removing HTML/noise, tokenization, stop-word removal and stemming or lemmatization. Bag of Words and TF-IDF are used for feature extraction; classifiers discussed include Naive Bayes, Logistic Regression and SVM. The proposed system emphasizes TF-IDF + Logistic Regression with SHAP-based word-level explanations and a dashboard for confidence scores and explanations; performance is evaluated with accuracy, precision, recall and F1-score.
Limitation of the Paper: Accuracy depends on training-data size, quality and diversity; false positives and false negatives remain possible; evolving/obfuscated/image-based spam can reduce effectiveness; frequent retraining increases maintenance cost; multilingual and mixed-language emails are challenging; explainability and privacy remain concerns.

Author Names: Maram Bani Younes; Ahmad Ababneh
Title of the Paper: Machine Learning Based Spam Detection in Digital Communication Systems: A Comparative Analysis
Dataset Used: Nine benchmarks across three platforms: Enron (28,063), TREC (83,446), SpamAssassin (6,048), Ling-Spam (2,859), UCI SMS (5,169), Nigara SMS (5,171), Kaggle SMS (10,286), Twitter (5,169) and YouTube (350).
Methodology Used: Uses public benchmark datasets for email, SMS and social media. Cleaning removes missing/duplicate records, normalizes text, removes punctuation/symbols and stopwords, and applies SMOTE to imbalanced training data. TF-IDF (top 500 features) is the primary representation. Six shallow ML classifiers—Naive Bayes, SVM, Random Forest, Decision Tree, KNN and Logistic Regression—are compared within-domain and across unseen datasets; additional experiments assess transformer-based sentence embeddings (DeBERTa).
Limitation of the Paper: Strong within-domain results degrade substantially on unseen/cross-domain datasets because of dataset and lexical distribution shifts. All datasets are English, limiting multilingual generalization. Individual models also have specific weaknesses such as RF overfitting, SVM computational cost and KNN weakness in high-dimensional spaces.

Author Names: Tiago A. Almeida; José María Gómez Hidalgo; Akebo Yamakami
Title of the Paper: Contributions to the Study of SMS Spam Filtering: New Collection and Results
Dataset Used: SMS Spam Collection: approximately 5,574 English SMS messages labeled ham/spam (about 4,827 ham and 747 spam).
Methodology Used: Introduces a public SMS spam corpus and evaluates established content-based classifiers. Multiple tokenization schemes are tested with linear SVM, several Naive Bayes variants, KNN, C4.5, boosted classifiers, PART and MDL. Performance is compared using Spam Caught, Blocked Hams, Accuracy and Matthews Correlation Coefficient; linear SVM provides the strongest baseline.
Limitation of the Paper: No dedicated limitation section is stated. The study is based on one relatively small English SMS corpus, so multilingual, temporal concept-drift and cross-corpus generalization are not evaluated.

Author Names: Serkan Ballı; Onur Karasoy
Title of the Paper: Development of Content-Based SMS Classification Application by Using Word2Vec-Based Feature Extraction
Dataset Used: SMS Spam Collection dataset.
Methodology Used: Builds a Word2Vec model from SMS content and structural message properties. New features measure message distances to spam- and ham-related words. These semantic/structural features are combined with traditional classifiers including Random Forest, MLP, SVM, Logistic Regression and Naive Bayes. Random Forest achieves about 99.64% accuracy.
Limitation of the Paper: No explicit limitation section is given. Evaluation is restricted to one English SMS benchmark, and the method is not externally validated on newer or cross-domain spam corpora.

Author Names: Luo GuangJun; Shah Nazir; Habib Ullah Khan; Amin Ul Haq
Title of the Paper: Spam Detection Approach for Secure Mobile Message Communication Using Machine Learning Algorithms
Dataset Used: SMS Spam Collection dataset; 70% training and 30% testing.
Methodology Used: Applies Logistic Regression, K-Nearest Neighbors and Decision Tree classifiers to ham/spam SMS classification. The dataset is split into training and testing sets and models are evaluated using accuracy, sensitivity and specificity. Logistic Regression reports the best performance at about 99% accuracy.
Limitation of the Paper: No formal limitation section is provided. The experimental scope is limited to a single SMS dataset and three classical classifiers, with no cross-dataset, multilingual or adversarial-spam validation.

Author Names: Pradeep Kumar Roy; Jyoti Prakash Singh; Snehasish Banerjee
Title of the Paper: Deep Learning to Filter SMS Spam
Dataset Used: UCI SMS Spam Collection benchmark: 747 spam and 4,827 non-spam messages.
Methodology Used: Compares classical ML classifiers (SGD, Naive Bayes, Logistic Regression, Random Forest and Gradient Boosting) with deep-learning CNN and LSTM models. CNN variants use dropout and 10-fold cross-validation; the best 3-CNN + dropout + 10-fold configuration reaches 99.44% accuracy.
Limitation of the Paper: The authors explicitly state that the work is dependent on English-language text messages only; performance on other languages and other spam domains remains for future research.

Author Names: Tian Xia; Xuemin Chen
Title of the Paper: A Weighted Feature Enhanced Hidden Markov Model for Spam SMS Filtering
Dataset Used: UCI SMS Spam Collection plus an additional Chinese SMS dataset for validation.
Methodology Used: After tokenization and stop-word removal, each word is weighted according to the difference between its distribution in spam and ham messages. Words are labeled using the sign of the weight and converted into an observation sequence for a discrete Hidden Markov Model. The method is compared with LSTM/CNN and assessed using precision, recall, F1, accuracy and AUC, with emphasis on fast training/filtering.
Limitation of the Paper: No dedicated limitation section is stated. The approach still depends on tokenization and word-distribution statistics and is tested mainly on the UCI benchmark plus one Chinese corpus; robustness to temporal concept drift and richer non-text spam is not established.

Author Names: C. Oswald; Sona Elza Simon; Arnab Bhattacharya
Title of the Paper: SpotSpam: Intention Analysis-Driven SMS Spam Detection Using BERT Embeddings
Dataset Used: SMS Spam Collection benchmark dataset.
Methodology Used: Uses 13 predefined intention labels to capture message semantics along with textual features. Contextual embeddings are generated using pretrained NLP/BERT-family models, intention scores are computed, and supervised classifiers are used to classify messages as spam or ham. The reported accuracy is about 98.07%, with precision and recall around 0.97.
Limitation of the Paper: The authors note that the accuracy is not the best among existing approaches. The method relies on a fixed set of 13 intention labels and a single benchmark dataset, so broader cross-domain and concept-drift behavior remains uncertain.

Author Names: Abdallah Ghourabi; Manar Alohaly
Title of the Paper: Enhancing Spam Message Classification and Detection Using Transformer-Based Embedding and Ensemble Learning
Dataset Used: SMS Spam Collection Dataset.
Methodology Used: Cleans SMS text and compares TF-IDF/word embeddings with BERT- and GPT-3-based representations. Four classifiers—SVM, KNN, CNN and LightGBM—are combined using an optimized weighted-voting ensemble. Experiments use an 80/20 train-test split and evaluate accuracy, precision, recall and F1-score; the ensemble with GPT-3 embeddings reaches about 99.91% accuracy.
Limitation of the Paper: The study evaluates English SMS messages only. The authors identify multilingual support as future work, so generalization to non-English spam is not demonstrated.

Author Names: Francisco Jáñez-Martino; Rocío Alaiz-Rodríguez; Víctor González-Castro; Eduardo Fidalgo; Enrique Alegre
Title of the Paper: A Review of Spam Email Detection: Analysis of Spammer Strategies and the Dataset Shift Problem
Dataset Used: Experimental study uses Ling-Spam, SpamAssassin, Enron-Spam, TREC07 and CSDMC; Bruce Guenter Spam Archive (2010 and 2018) is used for later/future-data testing.
Methodology Used: Combines a literature review of spammer/adversarial strategies with an empirical dataset-shift study. Four text-classification pipelines are formed from BOW or TF-IDF with Naive Bayes or SVM, trained on historical email datasets and tested across different corpora/time periods to quantify generalization degradation.
Limitation of the Paper: The empirical study is centered on selected classical text models and mostly historical English email corpora. The paper shows that public datasets from the 2000-2010 era can be unrepresentative of modern spam and that performance can deteriorate severely under dataset shift.

Author Names: Muhammad Adnan; Muhammad Osama Imam; Muhammad Furqan Javed; Iqbal Murtza
Title of the Paper: Improving Spam Email Classification Accuracy Using Ensemble Techniques: A Stacking Approach
Dataset Used: Combined SpamAssassin (6,047 messages) and a 7,582-message subsample of Enron-Spam; merged dataset contains 13,629 emails and is balanced by oversampling.
Methodology Used: Preprocesses subject/body text using NLTK and trains Logistic Regression, Decision Tree, Gaussian Naive Bayes, KNN and AdaBoost. Their probability outputs are stacked and passed to a Logistic Regression meta-classifier. Robustness is also checked by changing train/test sizes and base-classifier combinations; stacking achieves about 98.8% accuracy.
Limitation of the Paper: The authors identify the need for datasets containing image/personalized spam and emails manipulated by 'email warmer' tools. Continued evolution of spam may reduce effectiveness without new representative training data.

Author Names: Halim Asliyuksek; Ozgur Tonkal; Ramazan Kocaoglu
Title of the Paper: A Comparative Evaluation of a Multimodal Approach for Spam Email Classification Using DistilBERT and Structural Features
Dataset Used: Combined corpus of 81,586 emails from seven public spam datasets, including SpamAssassin variants, Enron-Spam, Ling-Spam, two Kaggle spam datasets and a spam-ham dataset used in prior Firefly-optimization research; 31,670 spam and 49,916 ham.
Methodology Used: All corpora are normalized to label/text fields and merged, then split stratified 80/20. Class imbalance is handled with random oversampling and class-weighted loss. Classical SVM, Random Forest, Naive Bayes and Logistic Regression are compared with DistilBERT and RoBERTa. A multimodal model fuses DistilBERT semantic representations with structural text features and includes threshold tuning plus temporal robustness analysis.
Limitation of the Paper: All datasets are English, restricting multilingual applicability. Adversarial training was not performed because of computational/time constraints, and ambiguous phishing or legitimate marketing language remains challenging.

Author Names: Ye Tian; Xin Dai; Zhijun Li; Hong Guo; Xiao Mao
Title of the Paper: Improving the Accuracy of Cybersecurity Spam Email Detection Using Ensemble Techniques: A Stacking Approach Machine Learning for Spam Email Detection
Dataset Used: Two publicly available sources are integrated: Kaggle email/SMS-style classification dataset with 5,572 samples and the Enron Corpus converted to a compatible category/message structure.
Methodology Used: Preprocessing includes cleaning, tokenization, lowercasing, stop-word removal, stemming/lemmatization and engineered length features. TF-IDF is used for textual representation, spam is oversampled to balance classes, and Naive Bayes, KNN, Logistic Regression and XGBoost are combined in a stacking framework with grid-search cross-validation and hyperparameter tuning.
Limitation of the Paper: The authors state that the training data are predominantly English and do not represent emerging AI-generated spam. Basic duplication-based oversampling can overfit, and ensemble models add computational cost; future work targets multilingual transfer, transformers and adversarial training.
